newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The rand succumbed to importer and offshore dollar demand as well as pressure from a resurgent dollar to end about a cent weaker on Wednesday in active trade.
At the 1400 GMT finish, the rand was pegged at 4.5500/5500 against the dollar after settling at 4.5390/5440 on Tuesday.

And cable's continuing rally pushed the rand to a fresh low of 7.2209 against sterling during the day before it recovered to 7.2113/2215 at the finish. Against the mark it was pegged at 0.3376/3381 from 0.3388/3392 previously.
Dealers said the currency began the day dipping below the 4.54 against the dollar level on initial exporter interest.
But that was soon met by importers and aggressive London-based demand for the greenback, which carried the rand to a morning high of 4.5500.

They said one of the reasons for the offshore dollar demand was a report released by Dutch bank ABN AMRO which said it expected the South African government was likely to abolish all remaining foreign exchange controls within two years.
The U.S. currency's resurgence against the Deutschmark and Japanese yen also contributed to the rand's woes.
Dealers said, however, that as the currency moved above the 4.55 level, both exporter and rumoured Reserve Bank dollar sales stemmed the currency's losses.
"It got quite hairy above the 4.55 level," one dealer said, adding that the currency's failure to move higher indicated it could firm a little on Thursday.
But some concern was expressed about rising forward rates.
Dealers said that the weaker rand, stronger dollar and rising NCD rates had all contributed to an increase in forward points.
Money market traders said the "slight cash squeeze" was a result of early commercial bank funding ahead of the traditionally volatile December period.
"A couple of banks want to get in funding for the December month when things are usually a bit tight," a dealer said. "Institutions are taking the paper, but not as much as expected."

He said the rise in short-term interest rates was insufficient, however, to bring pressure to bear on the shortage, which the Reserve Bank said eased to 7.641 billion rand on Tuesday from 7.940 billion rand on Monday.

Three-month NCDs rose to between 15.90 percent bid 16.05 percent offer from 15.85 to 16.00 percent on Tuesday, while 90-day BAs were also higher at between 15.35 and 15.45 percent from 15.30 and 15.40 percent previously.
The rise in money market rates also introduced an element of caution into the gilts market, where the yield on the key R150 stock rose to 15.28 percent at the finish from 15.205 percent previously.
"Some people are feeling that short-term rates have to come down first before we start moving down again," a dealer said.
For the most part, however, the market remained directionless and range-bound.
Hopes that U.S. September consumer inflation data would provide a pointer to the market were dashed when the figure matched market expectations with a 0.3 percent month-on-month rise.
Dealers said they expected the market to remain range-bound for the rest of the week, although a break above the 15.32 level could trigger further losses.
Bond Exchange figures show foreigners sold a net 31.81 million rand worth of South African bonds on Tuesday after selling 147.58 million rand worth on Monday.
Nominal cumulative volumes improved to 3.68 billion rand on Tuesday from a paltry 2.46 billion rand on Monday.
-- Paul Richardson, Johannesburg newsroom, +27 11 482-1003
